As we seat ourselves, it is with full anticipation that the ruler of the
synagogue will call on Jesus to deliver a discourse. Whenever "some great
Rabbi, or famed preacher, or else a distinguished stranger, is known to be in
the town," it is the custom to invite him to preach to the people. The
"institution of preaching" is a way of life among the Jews, and popular
preachers are sought for, and are given complete freedom to expound and
teach, using "parables, stories, allegories, witticisms, strange and foreign
words, absurd legends, in short, anything that might startle an audience."
We anticipate that, as is the custom, "at the close of his address, the
preacher" will refer "to the great Messianic hope of Israel," but little do we
realize the power and import of the Messianic proclamation that is to be
made this day.
